Apex Industrial Technologies Inc. - Q2 2024 Earnings Call Transcript

Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the Apex Industrial Technologies Inc. Q2 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are in listen-only mode. After the presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. If you would like to ask a question at that time, please press star then one on your touchtone phone. If using a speakerphone, please pick up your handset before pressing the keys. To withdraw your question, press star then two. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the call over to Sarah Jenkins, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Jenkins (Head of Investor Relations):
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to discuss Apex Industrial Technologies' results for the second quarter of 2024. Joining me on today's call are Michael Reynolds, Chief Executive Officer; David Patel, Chief Financial Officer; and Lisa Chen, Chief Operating Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements we will be making today are forward-looking in nature and subject to certain risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Michael Reynolds.

Michael Reynolds (CEO):
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. I'm pleased to report on Apex Industrial Technologies' performance for the second quarter of 2024. We've made significant progress on several fronts, delivering strong results amid a dynamic industrial landscape. Let me highlight a few key achievements.

First, our total order intake hit a robust $1.25 billion, up 26% year-over-year, reflecting exceptional demand across automation, aerospace, automotive, and energy sectors, with our backlog now at $3.2 billion providing clear visibility.

Second, we drove impressive organic revenue growth of 9%, complemented by meaningful inorganic contributions from strategic acquisitions like RoboForge Dynamics, underscoring the strength of our core operations and M&A execution.

Third, our automation and digital offerings segment surged 28% year-over-year, now 22% of total revenue, transforming customer efficiency through platforms like AutoFab Edge and digital twins, with recurring SaaS revenue up 42%.

Fourth, operationally, we've enhanced manufacturing efficiency via Industry 4.0 investments, reducing downtime and boosting OEE, while expanding capacity in key U.S. facilities to support reshoring.

Fifth, our share repurchase program advanced aggressively, with $785 million executed year-to-date, retiring 3.2% of shares and enhancing shareholder value in line with our capital allocation priorities.

We are confident that our strategic initiatives are positioning us for long-term sustainable growth in the $450 billion industrial equipment market.

Now, I'll turn the call over to David Patel to provide more detail on our financial results.

David Patel (CFO):
Thank you, Michael. Good afternoon, everyone. Thank you for joining our Q2 earnings call. I'll dive right into our top-line results, where we delivered consolidated revenue of $1.28 billion, up 15% year-over-year on a reported basis. Excluding the 2% foreign exchange headwind from a stronger U.S. dollar against the euro and yen, that's a robust 17% constant currency growth. As you know, we always break this down into organic and inorganic components to give you clear line-of-sight into the underlying momentum of our core operations versus bolt-on M&A activity.

Starting with organic revenue growth, which excludes acquisitions, divestitures, and FX, we achieved an impressive 9% increase. This marks the fifth consecutive quarter of double-digit organic growth in our core segments—Machinery & Automation and Aftermarket Services—outpacing the broader industrial equipment market, which we estimate grew around 4-5% globally per recent Gardner Intelligence data.

Let me unpack the drivers. Volume contributed 6 points, fueled by strong end-market demand across our key verticals. In semiconductors and electronics, which represent about 22% of our mix, we saw 18% organic growth, driven by capacity expansions at customers like TSMC and Intel fabs in the U.S. and Arizona. Our precision CNC machining centers and wafer handling systems benefited directly from this, with order intake up 25% sequentially. Automotive electrification was another bright spot—12% organic uptick—tied to EV battery gigafactory builds from the likes of Tesla and LG Energy Solution. Here, our high-precision robotic welders and assembly line automation solutions are gaining share, especially as OEMs push for faster cycle times and lighter-weight components.

Pricing added a solid 3 points to organic growth, reflecting our disciplined approach amid persistent inflation in steel, aluminum, and rare earths—inputs that make up 35% of our COGS. We implemented selective surcharges on 40% of our backlog earlier this year, similar to what peers like Applied Materials and Lam Research have done, without meaningful pushback thanks to our 95% on-time delivery rate.

Regionally, North America was the standout at 12% organic growth, propelled by reshoring trends under the CHIPS Act and Inflation Reduction Act. Our U.S. factories in Ohio and Texas are running at 92% utilization, with new IoT-enabled predictive maintenance tech reducing unplanned downtime by 28%—a key differentiator versus legacy players like Haas Automation. EMEA grew 5% organically but lagged due to energy costs compressing capex at European autos like Volkswagen and Stellantis. APAC delivered 8%, with strength in renewables; our wind turbine blade molding equipment saw 30% demand surge from offshore projects in Vietnam and Taiwan.

Aftermarket services, our highest-margin book at 42% incremental, grew 14% organically—nearly double the equipment sales rate—thanks to our ApexEdge platform. This SaaS-enabled fleet monitoring system, now live on 65% of our installed base, drove parts and service pull-through, mirroring the digital twin success we've seen at competitors like Siemens and Rockwell Automation.

Now, turning to the inorganic contribution from acquisitions, which added 6 points to total growth, or about $75 million in revenue. This was predominantly from our January close of the $450 million acquisition of RoboForge Dynamics, a leader in collaborative robot arms for industrial assembly. RoboForge contributed $68 million in Q2, right at the high end of our integration plan, with immediate synergies from cross-selling into our existing semiconductor and EV customers. We've already realized $12 million in run-rate cost savings through supply chain consolidation—streamlining their Asian sourcing with our U.S. hubs—and expect another $20 million from revenue synergies by year-end, including bundling their cobots with our CNC lathes for 'lights-out' manufacturing cells.

This deal fits squarely into our M&A playbook: tuck-ins under 2x EBITDA multiples that accelerate exposure to Industry 4.0 megatrends. Post-close, our automation backlog now stands at $2.1 billion, up 22% YoY, with RoboForge adding key IP in AI-driven path optimization. Smaller bolt-ons, like last quarter's $30 million purchase of a regional hydraulic pump specialist, chipped in the rest—about 1 point—bolstering our fluid power portfolio amid hydraulic-to-electric transitions in off-highway equipment.

Strategically, this organic/inorganic blend underscores our resilience in a fragmented $450 billion addressable market. Organic momentum validates our $500 million capex plan for 2024, focused on U.S. capacity adds and next-gen electric actuators compliant with EU carbon border taxes. Inorganic keeps us nimble—we've got $1.2 billion in dry powder for more deals targeting software-adjacent tuck-ins, especially in battery manufacturing where capex cycles mirror the semi boom of 2018-2020.

Looking forward, we expect Q3 organic growth of 8-10%, with full-year landing at 9-11%, even as we lap tougher comps. Total revenue growth should hit 14-16%, assuming stable FX. Risks remain around China real estate spillover and potential auto strikes, but our 55% aftermarket revenue mix and diversified verticals position us well.

Good afternoon, everyone. Thank you for joining our Q2 2024 earnings call for Apex Industrial Technologies. As your CFO, I'm thrilled to dive into one of our fastest-growing and highest-margin segments: our Automation and Digital Offerings portfolio. This area isn't just a growth engine—it's fundamentally transforming how our customers in the manufacturing and industrial equipment sectors operate, driving unprecedented efficiency gains amid persistent macroeconomic headwinds like inflation, labor shortages, and supply chain volatility.

Let me start with the headline numbers, which underscore the momentum here. In Q2, revenues from our Automation and Digital segment surged 28% year-over-year to $245 million, representing 22% of our total revenue—up from 17% a year ago. Bookings grew even faster at 35%, with a book-to-bill ratio of 1.28, signaling robust pipeline visibility into FY25. Recurring revenue from our software-as-a-service (SaaS) and managed services subscriptions hit $112 million, up 42% YoY, now accounting for 46% of segment sales. Margins expanded to 48.2%—nearly 1,300 basis points above our core hardware business—thanks to the high scalability of digital solutions and lower variable costs.

This growth is fueled by the broader Industry 4.0 megatrend, accelerated by post-pandemic digital transformation imperatives. According to McKinsey's latest Industrial Productivity Index, manufacturers adopting IIoT—Industrial Internet of Things—solutions are seeing 15-20% gains in Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE), and we're capturing that tailwind head-on. Our customers, from heavy machinery OEMs like Caterpillar and Deere analogs to semiconductor fab equipment makers, are prioritizing capex shifts toward automation to combat rising energy costs (up 12% globally per IEA data) and skilled labor gaps (projected at 2.1 million unfilled U.S. manufacturing jobs by 2030, per Deloitte).

At the core of our success are flagship offerings like our AutoFab Edge Platform and Predix-like Digital Twin Suite, which integrate AI, machine learning, and edge computing for real-time optimization. AutoFab, our modular automation suite, now deployed in over 1,200 factories worldwide, leverages NVIDIA Jetson edge AI modules for on-machine anomaly detection—reducing unplanned downtime by up to 35% through predictive maintenance algorithms trained on petabytes of proprietary sensor data.

A prime example: In Q2, we rolled out AutoFab 5G Connect, enabling ultra-low-latency wireless orchestration of cobots and AGVs (Automated Guided Vehicles) in high-mix, low-volume environments. This has been a game-changer for discrete manufacturers, with early adopters reporting 22% throughput improvements. Complementing this is our InsightAI Analytics, a cloud-native SaaS tool powered by partnerships with AWS and Siemens MindSphere, offering digital twins that simulate factory floor scenarios with 98% accuracy. Customers use it for virtual commissioning, slashing new line startup times from weeks to days.

We're also pioneering zero-touch automation via our Swarm Robotics Framework, inspired by ABB's YuMi but scaled for palletizing and kitting in logistics-heavy sectors like automotive Tier 1s. In pilot programs with EV battery assemblers, this has delivered 18% labor cost reductions while boosting OEE from 82% to 91%.

Geographically, we're seeing differentiated dynamics that align with regional industrial cycles. Americas (52% of segment revenue, +32% YoY): Reshoring and the CHIPS Act are supercharging demand. U.S. bookings jumped 40%, led by semiconductor equipment makers investing in fabs for Intel and TSMC's Arizona plants. A standout win: A $45 million, five-year contract with a leading CNC machine tool provider for AutoFab deployments across their Midwest facilities, promising 25% energy savings via AI-optimized spindle controls.

EMEA (28% of segment, +25% YoY): Energy transition and EU Green Deal mandates are key. German automotive OEMs, facing 15% natural gas cost hikes, adopted our Digital Twin Suite for heat pump production lines, yielding 28% efficiency gains. UK and Nordic wins in wind turbine nacelle assembly highlight our edge in renewable equipment automation.

APAC (20% of segment, +22% YoY): Semiconductor and EV hypergrowth persists despite China slowdowns. Taiwan and South Korea drove 45% bookings growth, with fabs like those mirroring ASML ecosystems integrating our IIoT sensors for 20% yield improvements. India's PLI scheme is opening doors, with Q2 pilots in steel rolling mills delivering 16% scrap rate reductions.

The real magic—and our competitive moat—is how these offerings deliver measurable efficiency ROI, fostering sticky, high-margin relationships. Across our 450+ reference customers, we've tracked aggregate impacts: Downtime Reduction: 32% average via predictive analytics, equating to $1.2 billion in annual customer savings (based on our telemetry data). OEE Uplift: +17% on average, with top-quartile implementations hitting 25% (benchmark: World Class OEE is 85%). Energy Efficiency: 22% reductions through ML-driven load balancing, critical as ESG pressures mount—our solutions helped clients cut Scope 2 emissions by 18% on average. Throughput and Yield: 19% gains in discrete assembly, vital for just-in-time models amid Red Sea disruptions.

For us, this translates to servitization: 65% of new deals include outcome-based pricing, like "pay-per-OEE-point" models, shifting from one-off capex to annuity streams. Customer Net Promoter Scores for digital hit 72, versus 54 for hardware, driving 28% upsell rates.

Strategically, we're doubling down on converged automation—blending OT (Operational Technology) with IT via open standards like OPC UA and ISA-95. Our $250 million R&D investment this year targets generative AI for autonomous factory tuning, akin to Rockwell's FactoryTalk Evolution, with beta launches in H1 2025. Partnerships with Microsoft Azure for hybrid edge-cloud and Bosch Rexroth for hydraulic-digital integration position us as the orchestrator in fragmented ecosystems.

Looking ahead, we guide FY24 segment growth at 26-30%, with recurring revenue exceeding 50% mix. Margins should sustain 47-49%, supporting EPS accretion. Risks like cyber vulnerabilities are mitigated via our ISO 27001-certified platform and zero-trust architecture. In summary, Automation and Digital isn't a silo—it's reshaping Apex Industrial Technologies into a solutions leader, delivering efficiency that customers can't replicate in-house. This positions us exceptionally for the $200 billion IIoT market opportunity through 2030, per Gartner.

Good afternoon, everyone. Before we open the line for Q&A, I'd like to provide a detailed update on our share repurchase program, which remains a cornerstone of our disciplined capital allocation framework here at Apex Industrial Technologies. As you know, we announced a $1.2 billion authorization in February 2024, following the completion of our prior $800 million program in late 2023. This reflects our strong conviction in the long-term value of our portfolio—from our core hydraulic presses and CNC machining centers to our growing electrification platforms like the E-Drive servo systems—amid an industrial capex upcycle driven by reshoring, automation, and infrastructure spending.

Program Execution to Date: Year-to-date through Q2, we've executed $785 million of repurchases, acquiring 4.8 million shares at an average price of $163.25 per share. This represents about 65% completion of the authorization, with a weighted average discount of 18% to our then-current intrinsic value estimates, based on our DCF models incorporating aftermarket service annuities and a 12-15% ROIC hurdle.

Breaking it down quarterly for transparency: Q1: $210 million (1.3 million shares at $161.50 avg.), opportunistic buys during the post-earnings dip tied to broader industrial PMI softness. Q2: $275 million (1.7 million shares at $162.00 avg.), accelerated as our order backlog grew 14% YoY to $3.2 billion, signaling strength in North American fab equipment demand. We've front-loaded aggressively, leveraging dips from Eurozone energy headwinds.

We've utilized a mix of open-market purchases under Rule 10b5-1 plans—about 70% of volume—and accelerated share repurchase (ASR) agreements with major banks like JPMorgan, which allowed us to collar 40% of Q2 volume at a VWAP discount. This technical structure minimizes market impact while maximizing accretion, with all repurchases funded from our $1.8 billion in trailing 12-month free cash flow generation. Post-execution, we've retired 3.2% of our diluted share count, from 285 million to 275.6 million shares outstanding, directly boosting diluted EPS by 3.4% on a pro forma basis for FY24 guidance.

In the Manufacturing & Industrial Equipment sector, buybacks like ours are increasingly common as peers navigate cyclical headwinds. Our trailing P/E of 14.2x trades at a 25% discount to the XLI ETF and below Caterpillar (CAT) at 16.8x or Deere (DE) at 15.4x, despite superior exposure to high-margin automation—our FANUC-integrated robotic welders now comprise 22% of mix, up from 15% in 2022. We've been undervalued due to transitory factors: global ISM Manufacturing Index hovering at 48.5 in Q2, China fab utilization down 8% amid EV overcapacity, and lingering supply chain frictions from Red Sea disruptions inflating alloy steel costs by 12%.

That said, leading indicators point to inflection: U.S. industrial capex up 7% YoY per Census data, fueled by the IIJA's $550 billion outlay creating tailwinds for our infrastructure-grade excavator attachments. Europe, representing 28% of revenue, saw softer execution but we're resuming with German Industrie 4.0 subsidies boosting orders for our Siemens-partnered IoT-enabled lathes.

Regionally, North America (62% of repurchases) benefits from onshoring—think Intel's $20B Ohio fab driving demand for our precision grinders. Asia-Pacific (22%) slowed slightly, prioritizing backlog conversion over buys amid Taiwan semi tensions, while EMEA (16%) focused on high-conviction dips post-Brexit supply normalization.

Strategically, this program underscores our capital hierarchy: 40% to dividends (recently hiked 8% to $1.28/share), 30% to buybacks, 20% debt reduction (net debt/EBITDA at 1.8x), and 10% tuck-in M&A like our Q2 acquisition of a Danish fiber laser firm to electrify our cutting tools portfolio. Buybacks offset 85% of equity comp dilution and signal confidence in mid-teens EPS growth through the cycle, as aftermarket services (35% of EBITDA margins) derisk volatility. We've modeled 10-15% accretion annually at current valuations, enhancing TSR versus buy-and-hold peers like Ingersoll Rand (IR).

We have $415 million remaining under authorization, with $250-300 million planned for H2, contingent on stock pricing below $170 and sustained FCF of $500 million quarterly. No plans for extension yet, but we'll reassess post-earnings if industrial production ex-auto exceeds 2.5% YoY. This remains opportunistic, not programmatic, tied to our $4.5 billion liquidity position and A- credit profile. In summary, our repurchase execution has been precise, value-accretive, and aligned with Apex Industrial Technologies' leadership in next-gen industrial equipment. We're returning capital efficiently while positioning for the automation megatrend.

Good afternoon, everyone. Thank you for joining our Q2 earnings call. As we dive into the financials, I'd like to start with one of our key leading indicators: total order intake, which came in at $1.25 billion for the quarter, representing a robust 26% year-over-year growth from $992 million in Q2 FY2023. This marks our strongest quarterly order intake since Q4 FY2021, pre-COVID peaks, and underscores the structural tailwinds we're capturing across our core end-markets in aerospace, automotive, semiconductors, and industrial automation.

To put this in context, our trailing 12-month order intake now stands at $4.7 billion, up 22% YoY, with our book-to-bill ratio expanding to 1.18x—well above our long-term target of 1.10x. This healthy ratio reflects not just top-of-funnel demand strength but also our ability to convert inquiries into firm orders, supported by our expanded engineering services and value-added solutions. Our ending backlog grew 18% YoY to $3.2 billion, providing excellent revenue visibility into FY2025 and beyond, with approximately 65% expected to convert within the next 12 months.

Let me break this down by segment, as the growth story is multifaceted and tied to specific industry dynamics. Automation & Robotics Division (45% of total intake): Orders here surged 38% YoY to $560 million, driven by hyperscaler investments in semiconductor fabrication and data center buildouts. We're seeing accelerated adoption of our AeroFlex modular robotic cells, which integrate AI-powered vision systems and collaborative robots—similar to what's powering Fanuc and ABB deployments but optimized for high-mix, low-volume precision machining. Key wins included a $120 million follow-on order from a leading U.S. chipmaker akin to TSMC's Arizona fab expansion, where our systems enable 30% faster die attach and wire bonding processes. Margins on these are accretive at 28% gross, thanks to our in-house machine learning algorithms for predictive throughput optimization.

Aerospace & Defense (30% of intake): Intake reached $375 million, up 22% YoY, fueled by commercial aviation recovery and defense spending ramps. Boeing and Airbus production cadence improvements—now targeting 50+ 737 MAX and A320neo per month—have unlocked orders for our TitanForge titanium forging presses and HyperMill 5-axis CNC machining centers. A standout was a $85 million multi-year deal with a Tier-1 supplier for widebody engine casings, leveraging our proprietary vacuum arc remelting tech that reduces material waste by 15% versus legacy methods. Geopolitically, U.S. DoD budget hikes under the FY2024 NDAA have boosted aftermarket upgrades, contributing 12% of this segment's growth.

Automotive & EV (15% of intake): We posted 15% YoY growth to $190 million, somewhat tempered by inventory destocking in legacy ICE vehicles but offset by EV structural shifts. Orders for our ElectroPress battery cell forming equipment—capable of 20% higher throughput for solid-state cathodes—came from players like Tesla's Nevada Gigafactory and a European OEM mirroring Volkswagen's ID. series ramp. Our strategic pivot to gigacasting solutions, inspired by Giga Press adopters like IDRA, positioned us for a $50 million order in structural aluminum die casting.

Industrial & Energy (10% of intake): This bucket grew 12% YoY to $125 million, with renewables leading via wind turbine nacelle gear systems and hydrogen electrolyzer skids. Wins here mirror Siemens Gamesa's offshore wind orders, where our high-torque helical gearboxes deliver 25% better efficiency under IEC Class S standards.

Regionally, the U.S. and North America accounted for 52% of intake at $650 million (up 32% YoY), propelled by CHIPS Act funding—over $50 billion allocated—and onshoring trends. Mexico's nearshoring boom added tailwinds, with maquiladora expansions mirroring Foxconn's investments. Europe contributed 28% or $350 million (up 18% YoY), buoyed by the EU Green Deal's €1 trillion mobilization for net-zero manufacturing; our compliance with REACH and RoHS via sustainable alloys has been a differentiator. APAC was 18% at $225 million (up 14% YoY), with China EV overcapacity pressuring but India and Southeast Asia offsetting via semiconductor diversification—think Applied Materials' ecosystem.

Technically, our Industry 4.0 initiatives are proving pivotal. We've rolled out digital twin-enabled order configuration tools across our sales force, reducing quote-to-order cycles by 40% and boosting win rates to 35% from 28% YoY. Investments in edge computing for real-time MES integration—compatible with Rockwell Automation's FactoryTalk and Siemens' MindSphere—have differentiated us in capex-constrained environments. Sustainability is embedded too: 75% of new orders specify low-carbon steel forgings, aligning with Scope 3 emissions mandates.

Strategically, this order momentum validates our 'Forge Forward' initiative—$250 million CapEx over two years in U.S. capacity expansion, including our new 500,000 sq ft facility in Ohio for reshoring CNC production. We're derisking supply chains post-2022 disruptions, with 90% North American sourcing for critical components versus 65% in FY2022. Pricing discipline held firm, with a 4.2% realization on renewals, countering steel input inflation now stabilizing at 2% QoQ.

Looking ahead, our Q3 order intake guide is $1.3 to $1.4 billion, implying FY2024 full-year growth of 24% to $5.1 billion. Risks include auto cyclicality and potential Fed pauses on rate cuts impacting capex, but our exposure to megatrends—semis (projected 15% CAGR), aero (20% backlog growth at OEMs), and automation (IIoT market to $500B by 2028 per McKinsey)—positions us resiliently. We're maintaining our FY2025 revenue growth outlook of 15-18%, with order intake as the North Star.

Turning to our broader financial performance, gross margin was 38.5%, driven by favorable product mix from high-margin automation sales, pricing actions, and manufacturing efficiencies. Operating expenses were $285 million, resulting in an operating income of $210 million. Our net income for the quarter was $145 million, or $0.52 per share.

Thank you, Michael. Now, let me dive into the key assumptions underpinning our FY2024 guidance, which calls for revenue growth of 12-14% year-over-year to a range of $5.1-5.25 billion, adjusted EBITDA margins expanding 150 basis points to 22-23%, and non-GAAP EPS of $5.75-6.10. These targets reflect a balanced view of macroeconomic tailwinds, resilient end-market demand, and our strategic execution in high-growth areas like factory automation and electrification. I'll break this down by macro environment, end-market dynamics, regional nuances, and operational levers, while highlighting the sensitivities.

Macroeconomic Backdrop: Our guidance assumes moderate global GDP growth of 2.8% in 2024, in line with IMF projections, with U.S. real GDP at 2.4%, Eurozone at 1.2%, and China at 4.6%. This supports a constructive capex cycle, as industrial PMIs stabilize above 50—U.S. ISM Manufacturing at 51, Eurozone at 49.5 recovering to 50.5 by year-end. We expect U.S. inflation to cool to 2.2% CPI, easing input cost pressures on steel, copper, and semiconductors, which comprise ~25% of our COGS. However, we're baking in a 50 bps risk to our top line from persistent supply chain frictions, such as Red Sea disruptions adding 2-3% to ocean freight costs.

End-Market Demand Assumptions: Demand visibility remains strong, with our Q2 book-to-bill ratio at 1.25x—up from 1.15x last year—signaling backlog conversion into revenue. We're assuming: Factory Automation (42% of revenue): 10-12% growth, driven by AI-enabled cobots and collaborative robots akin to Universal Robots' UR series. End-user capex for Industry 4.0 digital twins and edge computing is projected to rise 15%, fueled by labor shortages and productivity mandates. Utilization rates in automotive and consumer electronics plants are expected at 85-88%. Semiconductor & Electronics Equipment (18% of revenue): 12-15% uplift, mirroring ASML and Applied Materials' fab expansion cycles. We're assuming global wafer fab equipment spend hits $110 billion (per SEMI), with AI data center builds—think Nvidia GPU ramps—boosting demand for our precision motion control systems and wafer handling robots. Aerospace & Defense (15% of revenue): Steady 6-8% growth, supported by Boeing and Airbus backlogs exceeding 15,000 aircraft. U.S. DoD budgets at $850 billion underpin aftermarket MRO services for our CNC machining centers. Construction & Mining (12% of revenue): Flat to +2%, as high interest rates cap non-residential starts, but offset by infrastructure bills like the U.S. IIJA ($1.2 trillion through 2026). We're modeling Komatsu-like hydraulic excavator demand tied to copper mine expansions for electrification. Other (13%): Energy transition tailwinds, with oil & gas holding flat amid OPEC+ cuts, but renewables up 20% via wind turbine gearboxes and EV battery assembly lines.

Regional Commentary: North America (45% of revenue): Core growth engine at 9-11%, propelled by reshoring and CHIPS Act subsidies ($52 billion). Onshoring in semiconductors and EVs—e.g., Intel's Ohio fabs and Tesla's Texas Gigafactory—drives 25% order growth in our motion control segment. Europe (25%): Modest 4-6% growth, challenged by energy costs (still 20% above pre-Ukraine levels) and German auto slowdowns at VW and BMW. Upside from REPowerEU green capex, targeting 15% electrification in industrial gearmotors. Asia-Pacific (25%): Highest growth at 10-13%, led by China's "Made in China 2025" push into high-end CNCs and India's PLI scheme for electronics manufacturing. Taiwan semis remain robust, but we're assuming a 5% FX headwind from a stronger USD. Rest of World (5%): LatAm mining capex up 8% on lithium for EVs.

Strategic Insights and Technical Initiatives: Our edge comes from proactive derisking. We've embedded 3-5% margin accretion from our "SmartFactory" platform—IoT-enabled predictive maintenance reducing downtime 25% via ML algorithms, similar to Rockwell Automation's FactoryTalk. Electrification initiatives, like SiC-based inverters for 800V EV architectures, position us for 20% CAGR in that subsegment through 2030. Supply chain resilience includes dual-sourcing critical rare earths (80% non-China by Q2) and a $150 million inventory build for lead times normalizing to 12-14 weeks.

Sensitivities and Risks: This guidance assumes no recession— a 1% GDP shortfall could shave 300 bps off revenue growth. Upside levers: stronger semis capex (+200 bps to EPS) or M&A tuck-ins like our recent $200 million bolt-on in cobot tech. Downside: geopolitical flares (e.g., Taiwan tensions) or steel tariffs >25%. We'll monitor quarterly via customer SIPOC surveys and adjust dynamically.

In summary, our assumptions reflect a "soft landing" with structural tailwinds in automation and sustainability, giving us conviction in delivering the upper half of guidance. We are reaffirming our guidance for the full year, with expected revenue growth of 12-14% and EPS of $5.75-6.10. We are committed to returning capital to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases.

Now, I will hand over to Lisa Chen, COO, for an operational update.

Lisa Chen (COO):
Thank you, David. Operationally, we've been focused on streamlining our supply chain and improving manufacturing efficiency. Building on the automation momentum David outlined, we've implemented several new initiatives like the AutoFab Edge rollout and digital twin integrations that are already yielding positive results—downtime down 32% on average, OEE up 17%, and energy use reduced 22% across key sites. Our Ohio and Texas facilities are at 92% utilization, supported by dual-sourced rare earths and 90% North American critical components. We are closely monitoring the global supply chain situation, including Red Sea impacts, and taking proactive steps like inventory builds and vendor diversification to mitigate any potential disruptions. We are also investing in automation and digital technologies, including $250 million in R&D for generative AI factory tuning, to enhance our operational capabilities and support the 26-30% growth in our digital segment.

Operator:
Thank you. We will now begin the question-and-answer session. If you would like to ask a question, please press star then one. Our first question comes from John Smith with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

John Smith (Goldman Sachs):
Good morning. Can you discuss the impact of rising raw material costs on your profitability?

David Patel:
Thanks, John. We've managed this effectively through our pricing discipline, which contributed 3 points to organic growth this quarter. Amid inflation in steel, aluminum, and rare earths—key inputs at 35% of COGS—we rolled out selective surcharges on 40% of our backlog, similar to peers, with no pushback given our 95% on-time delivery. Combined with mix shift to 48% margins in automation and efficiencies from predictive maintenance cutting downtime 28%, our gross margin expanded to 38.5%. We're hedged on 60% of Q3 needs and see stabilization ahead, supporting our margin guidance.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Emily Rodriguez with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Emily Rodriguez (JPMorgan):
What is your outlook for demand in the aftermarket services business?

Michael Reynolds:
Great question, Emily. Aftermarket remains a standout, growing 14% organically—double the equipment rate—and now 55% of revenue with 42% incremental margins. Our ApexEdge SaaS platform, live on 65% of the installed base, is driving parts pull-through via fleet monitoring, much like Siemens' digital twins. With backlog conversion strong and servitization in 65% of deals, including pay-per-OEE models, we see sustained double-digit growth, derisking cyclicality and fueling EPS through annuity streams. Regional strength in North America reshoring adds further tailwinds.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Mike Thompson with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Mike Thompson (Morgan Stanley):
Can you provide an update on your progress in reducing lead times?

Lisa Chen:
Absolutely, Mike. We've made solid strides, normalizing to 12-14 weeks via our Forge Forward CapEx, including the new Ohio facility, and Industry 4.0 tools like digital twin order config, which cut quote-to-order 40%. Edge computing MES integrations with FactoryTalk and MindSphere boost win rates 35%, while dual-sourcing hits 90% North American for critical parts.
